text: This chapter has been building toward something real: a production bug. The Regional Manager emails that category breakdown for Store 48 on March 2nd adds up to one number, and the Store Ops dashboard shows a completely different total for that exact same store and day. Those two tables are supposed to be the same pipeline. Which one is right isn't something to answer by eyeballing a dashboard.

The first job isn't fixing anything, it's reproducing the problem reliably. Lesson 9 already built the right tool for this: the reconciliation query comparing daily_sales_summary against a rolled-up category_breakdown. Run it again, unmodified, filtered to the exact store and day reported.

Run it for real, and it comes back with one row: fifteen thousand, three hundred forty-two dollars and eighteen cents in daily_sales_summary, against thirteen thousand, eight hundred ninety-seven fifty-two in the rolled-up category breakdown. A gap of fourteen hundred forty-four dollars. Lesson 9's tolerance is one cent. This isn't rounding noise. The report is confirmed.

A single bad row tells you something is wrong, not when it started going wrong. So isolate the variable: widen the same query to a date range, grouped by day, for that same store, and look at the shape of the problem instead of one data point.

Here's the real tell. Every day from February 15th through February 29th comes back clean, zero difference, exactly as it should. Starting March 1st, every single day shows a nonzero gap, and the gaps only grow from there. A discrepancy that starts cleanly on one specific date isn't random drift, it's the signature of a change that went live right around that date.

That's a lead, not a conclusion. You haven't opened the MERGE job yet, and nothing gets touched until the real cause is confirmed. Next lesson follows this exact lead, Store 48, the date it started, straight to the line of code responsible.
